By my second morning on Oʻahu, I had sand in my sandals, a favorite breakfast spot, and a habit of checking the ocean before checking my phone. My recent trip to Hawaiʻi took me from Honolulu’s busy waterfront to the volcanic landscapes of Hawaiʻi Island, with plenty of stops for food, history, and spontaneous beach time.

What has stayed with me most is how much there was to learn between those postcard views.

Waikīkī made an irresistible starting point. Early in the morning, the beach felt wonderfully unhurried: surfers paddled toward the break, swimmers slipped into the water, and Diamond Head rose above the shoreline. One evening, I watched the sunset turn the water copper while the beachfront slowly filled with people enjoying the same simple ritual.

For a different perspective, I hiked Lēʻahi, also known as Diamond Head. The climb brought switchbacks, stairs, and plenty of reasons to pause for water. At the summit, Honolulu stretched along the coast, framed by an ocean that seemed to change color every few seconds. It deserves its place on an Oʻahu itinerary; check current reservation requirements before going, and aim for an early start.

Downtown Honolulu offered another essential stop: ʻIolani Palace. Walking through the former royal residence and learning about the Hawaiian Kingdom, its monarchs, and the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893 gave the trip a deeper historical context. Leave yourself time to listen and absorb the stories here.

A hula performance became another memorable part of my stay. Explanations of the mele—the songs or chants—helped me appreciate how movement and language convey stories and relationships to place. Understanding even a little of what I was watching made me pay closer attention to every gesture.

Food provided its own invitation to explore. I loved the contrast between cool, savory poke after a warm morning outside and a generous plate lunch after an afternoon of walking. A meal of kālua pork, laulau, and poi introduced me to traditional Hawaiian foods, while shave ice supplied a particularly welcome afternoon break. Hawaiʻi’s food also reflects generations of migration, with Japanese, Chinese, Filipino, Portuguese, and other influences woven through everyday menus.

On Oʻahu’s North Shore, I slowed down. Haleʻiwa offered an easy place to wander, find lunch, and linger before heading toward the beaches. Watching the surf was an attraction in itself. Ocean conditions vary enormously with the season, so build your beach plans around local conditions and lifeguard guidance.

Then came Hawaiʻi Island, where the landscape changed dramatically.

At Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, I followed trails through lava terrain and stopped at overlooks across Kīlauea’s immense volcanic landscape. Walking through Nāhuku, a lava tube surrounded by lush forest, was especially striking: one moment beneath green foliage, the next inside a passage formed by flowing lava.

Kīlauea also holds profound cultural significance and is associated with Pele in Hawaiian tradition. That context made taking time with the park’s exhibits as rewarding as the walks. Check current park conditions before visiting; access and volcanic activity can change, and visible lava is never guaranteed.

At Punaluʻu Black Sand Beach, I lingered over the contrast of dark sand, white surf, and green sea turtles resting near the water. I gave the turtles plenty of space and found a quiet spot to sit.

On my final evening, I stayed by the shoreline until the light faded. There were still places on my list, but for once I felt no urge to hurry toward the next one."}
